item.title: The Multi-Layered Nature of Wireless Audio Security: From Firmware Vulnerabilities to Chipset Risks
item.description: This article reveals that wireless earbuds have evolved from ordinary accessories into micro-terminals with computing capabilities. Subtle timing vulnerabilities in firmware pairing logic, such as Beats' CVE-2025-20701 and Airoha chipset flaws, can be exploited for unauthorized eavesdropping and tracking. By analyzing cross-layer security blind spots ranging from chip SDKs to auto-pairing protocols, the article warns the industry to integrate wearable audio devices into core endpoint defense systems.

item.title: CVSS 9.9 uutils Coreutils Vulnerability: Translation File Injection Leads to Rust Code Execution
item.description: This article exposes a severe CVSS 9.9 supply chain vulnerability in the Rust core utility library uutils, where attackers can implant malicious code at compile time by injecting specific characters into translation files. Given that uutils has become the default toolset for mainstream Linux distributions with massive download volumes, this discovery highlights how seemingly harmless localization files can serve as high-risk entry points for system-level backdoors, necessitating immediate upgrades and fixes.

item.title: Google Issues Chrome Security Update for Eighth Actively Exploited Zero-Day of 2026
item.description: Google on Monday released updates to patch nine security vulnerabilities, including one that has come under active exploitation in the wild. The high-severity vulnerability, assigned the CVE identifier CVE-2026-125350 (CVSS score: N/A), has been described as a use-after-free bug in the XML component. Use-after-free bugs typically occur when a program attempts to access a memory location after it has already been freed. Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to achieve data corruption, program crashes, or arbitrary code execution. An anonymous security researcher has been credited with discovering and reporting the flaw on November 6, 2026. Google acknowledged it is "aware that an exploit for CVE-2026-125350 exists in the wild," but has not revealed any additional specific information related to how it's being abused in real-world attacks or who is behind them. item.title: Hackers Exploit Qubole's Trusted AWS Access to Breach Customer Accounts and Steal Data
item.description: An attacker broke into AWS accounts belonging to multiple Qubole customers between October 14 and October 26 and stole stored secrets and data, cloud security company Wiz said today. The attacker used credentials for an AWS account that Qubole's platform uses to reach those customers. How the attacker got those credentials has not been disclosed. Qubole , a data lake platform owned by Idera, operates within its customers' AWS accounts. To let it in, a customer creates an IAM role, which is an AWS identity with its own set of permissions. The role's trust policy allows Qubole's AWS account to assume the role, granting those permissions. Each request to do this, called AssumeRole , must include a matching code from Qubole known as an External ID. Apart from the attack, most of the roles the attacker assumed were unused, according to Wiz's researchers. But each role still trusted Qubole's account, so the attacker's requests worked. Any organization...

item.title: Hackers Compromise Ethersphere's bee-js and Swarm Desktop to Deliver Wallet-Stealing Malware
item.description: Attackers used the Ethersphere project's own release automation to publish malicious versions of two of its tools for the Swarm decentralized storage network: bee-js 13.3.0 and Swarm Desktop 0.56.2. Both releases download and run code built to steal the wallet key that Swarm Desktop keeps for its node, along with the stored password that unlocks it. The code is also built to install a backdoor on Windows, macOS, and Linux machines. The bee-js package is the JavaScript library behind Swarm Desktop and the swarm-cli command-line tool. Swarm Desktop runs a Swarm node on a user's own computer and saves the node's private keys there. Both malicious releases have been taken down, and the project's maintainers released a clean Swarm Desktop update today. Neither step removes a backdoor already installed nor protects a key already sent. No theft of funds had been reported at the time of writing. "PapRAT has both C++ and Rust implementations," Fortinet FortiGuard Labs researcher Cara Lin said . item.description: A system doesn't always need a complicated bug to let someone in. Sometimes, a blank password is enough. That's one of the bigger stories this week. And it gets worse when the tools meant to keep systems updated or running safely become part of the attack. Elsewhere, attackers are hiding inside normal web traffic, stealing credentials from network devices, and finding new uses for exposed systems. AI is helping some of them move faster, but old mistakes are doing plenty of the work too. Even forgotten settings and small changes made months ago are coming back to cause trouble. item.title: Default 'admin:admin' Server Password Helps Researchers Hack Two Automakers, Unlock and Start Cars
item.description: The login systems behind two car brands' mobile apps could be taken over completely, two security researchers found, allowing them to access any customer's account and, for an owner with a connected car, unlock the doors and start the engine. Both apps signed customers in through ForgeRock , an identity platform now part of Ping Identity , and on those servers the researchers reached an administrator console that still used its default password. They tested the full attack only on their own and consenting owners' cars in the United States, in February 2026, and both systems were fixed about two hours after they reported the problem. Shubham Shah and Sam Curry published their work late last week. They had started with the apps: both brands signed customers in through the same platform, which runs in two parts: one for login and one, called OpenIDM , that holds customer records. OpenIDM comes with a built-in administrator console powered by the Apache Felix tool. For...

item.title: Web3Auth Flaw Exploited to Steal Keplr Crypto, Provider Empties Other Wallets for Safety
item.description: Some people who set up a Keplr crypto wallet with their Google or Apple account have had money stolen by an attacker. Keplr uses a company called Web3Auth to run that Google and Apple sign-in. The attacker used a security flaw at that company to reach the wallets, both companies said late last week. Web3Auth then used the attacker's own route to empty other at-risk wallets before the attacker got to them, it said. It moved that money, with help from the wallet maker, into recovery wallets for safekeeping. So an empty balance may mean the money was rescued, not stolen. Wallets made with a recovery phrase (a backup list of 12 or 24 words) or a hardware wallet are not affected, the wallet maker said. It has paused Google and Apple sign-in while it investigates. What Affected Users Should Do The wallet maker has given this user guidance for accounts created with Google or Apple login: Do not send new funds to the account. item.title: LNbits Urges All Operators to Shut Down Their Bitcoin Lightning Wallet Servers Amid Attacks
item.description: Everyone running LNbits , a free, open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet system, should shut down their servers now because of a wave of attacks, the project said yesterday. It has several security fixes to release and asked operators to be careful until they are out. One operator said new accounts used an exploit to withdraw 2,285,545 satoshis, about 0.023 bitcoin, from his server before he could stop it. The shutdown notice came about 80 minutes after a first, narrower warning. That warning asked operators to disable Paywall, an add-on that makes people pay to view content, while the project looked into a possible bug. As of 09:00 UTC today, the project had not released a fixed version. On X, it had not canceled the notice, offered another option, or told operators how to check whether their servers were hit before they were shut down. item.title: Taiwan-Based Hacker Used BOSSAI AI Agents to Steal Taipei Emergency Dispatch Records
item.description: A single attacker using AI agents pulled emergency dispatch records covering seven Taipei districts, researchers at Acronis's Threat Research Unit said last week. The agents also found a Taipei fire department platform exposing patient data from 2018, including ECG readings and ambulance video footage, without a login. The researchers are highly confident that the attacker is a single person based in Hualien City, Taiwan. He aimed the agents at hundreds of organizations in at least 11 countries, including emergency services, banks, universities and military systems. The agents collected data or accessed systems at about 10 of them in Taiwan, Mexico and Thailand. The evidence comes from the attacker's own server, which initially appeared to be a misconfigured development system.
